part_title: Amazon S3 Vectors and Bedrock Knowledge Bases

scenes.title: Amazon S3 Vectors
scenes.narration: Amazon S3 Vectors provides a way to store and query vector embeddings at scale using a vector bucket. Look at the four stages across the diagram. First, an application creates an S3 vector bucket for vector data. Second, it configures a vector index, including the dimensions and distance metric appropriate to the chosen embeddings. Third, it stores vector records together with keys and optional metadata. Fourth, the application queries for nearest vectors. Notice the example query result: the service returns matching vector identifiers and useful metadata, which can help the application find the related source documents. The lower panel emphasizes S3 Vectors' scale and cost-oriented design for large collections. It doesn't mean that every query pattern or advanced search feature supported by OpenSearch is also present in S3 Vectors. For a real architecture, decide whether the workload needs primarily durable, economical semantic search or additional features such as hybrid retrieval, advanced aggregations and filtering.

scenes.title: Put Vectors: Payload Shape
scenes.narration: This is a concrete API data-shape slide, so follow the JSON example carefully. The request identifies a vector bucket and a vector index. Under vectors, each item has its own key, a float thirty-two vector representation, and optional metadata. The first example represents a product record; its metadata includes a source and category. The second represents a support document and labels it accordingly. Follow the arrow from the JSON request to the vector bucket and its product index. The storage illustration on the right confirms that the records retain their separate keys, embeddings and metadata fields. A developer must ensure that all vectors written to the index use the expected dimensions and valid data types. The same index must use embeddings compatible with the query embedding model. The JSON shown here is an instructional example of the request structure, not a license to copy the sample's short vectors into a production index configured for hundreds or thousands of dimensions.

scenes.title: Ways to Ingest and Query Vectors
scenes.narration: This slide shows two ingestion choices and one query path. In the first path, the application reads source content, invokes an embedding model itself, and writes the resulting vectors through the S3 Vectors APIs. The application controls chunking, embedding selection and metadata. In the second path, an ingestion helper or script performs embedding generation and storage with Amazon Bedrock, while the application supplies the source files. Both paths ultimately write vectors to a compatible S3 vector index. Now look at the lower query row. A user asks a natural-language question. The application converts that question into a vector using a compatible embedding model, submits a nearest-neighbour query to S3 Vectors, and receives relevant vector identifiers or metadata. Those results can lead to the underlying text passages for a grounded response. The design choice is how much of indexing and embedding management you want in your own application. Maintain consistent embedding dimensions and authorization across the entire flow.

scenes.title: Bedrock Knowledge Bases with S3 Vectors
scenes.narration: This slide contrasts two integration patterns. At the top, Bedrock Knowledge Bases manages the ingestion workflow from supported source content. It performs chunking, generates embeddings and stores vector representations in S3 Vectors, when configured as a supported vector store. A user query then retrieves relevant evidence and supplies context to a generation model. Follow the bottom pattern for comparison: your application manages its own chunking, embeddings and S3 Vectors index directly, then uses retrieved content in a Bedrock model request. The two options can lead to similar retrieval results, but the engineering responsibility is different. With a managed Knowledge Base, the service handles more of the ingestion and indexing lifecycle. With application-managed vectors, the team owns the pipeline and retrieval implementation. The yellow note at the bottom stresses the integration choice: S3 Vectors is vector storage and retrieval, while Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides higher-level managed RAG functionality. Neither path removes the need for evaluation, data permissions or source freshness.

scenes.title: Choosing a Vector Retrieval Tier
scenes.narration: Now compare two search tiers for different requirements. The left panel presents Amazon S3 Vectors as a cost-oriented option for storing very large collections of vectors and metadata, with similarity queries. The right panel shows OpenSearch, which supports richer search functions such as keyword-plus-vector hybrid retrieval, aggregations and additional filtering options depending on the deployment. Look at the lower diagram: an S3 vector index snapshot may be exported or used as a source for an OpenSearch-oriented workflow where supported, creating a separate copy of the vector data. A copy increases both flexibility and storage responsibility; the two indexes do not magically stay synchronized. The orange note reminds us to select on business need. If large-scale economical vector retrieval is enough, S3 Vectors may be appropriate. If the application demands rich hybrid queries and search analysis, OpenSearch may justify its greater operational and cost considerations. Test the actual capabilities, data access patterns, latency and pricing before deciding.

scenes.title: S3 Vectors Operating Practices
scenes.narration: Let's finish with the operating practices illustrated here. The left column begins with batch writes when practical: grouping operations can be more efficient than issuing large numbers of tiny requests. Next, throttled queries should be retried with exponential backoff rather than repeated immediately. Third, the slide recommends separating indexes when workloads, security boundaries or metadata needs differ. Fourth, it says to mark metadata non-filterable when that metadata is needed only in returned results, not as a query filter, where supported by the index configuration. Now study the multi-tenant diagram on the right. Tenant A, B and C have separate IAM policies and vector indexes so access can be scoped explicitly. The query router should never mix authorized and unauthorized tenant data in one result. For real deployments, check authorization at the caller, bucket and index layers, as applicable. This lecture concludes our first introduction to S3 Vectors. The next topic will cover relational databases and Amazon Aurora in AI applications.
